newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin seeks help for Russia's cheated investors.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin seeks help for Russia's cheated investors.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin told Russia's government on Tuesday to do more to end wage delays and to help millions of people who lost their savings in dubious investment schemes.

Yeltsin, in a public show of concern for the social and economic problems behind nationwide protests that have been called for Thursday, also said he was setting up a special fund to help war veterans and pensioners deal with their problems.
"I consider the situation with the mass delays in wage payments unbearable," presidential press secretary Sergei Yastrzhembsky quoted Yeltsin as saying.
Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing that Yeltsin would discuss the problems on Wednesday with Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin and first deputy prime ministers Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov.
He said better coordination was needed between leaders in Moscow, the authorities in the regions and trade unions.

Yeltsin appeared to be keen to show, on the eve of the planned nationwide protests over government economic policy, that he is trying to deal with the problems causing most discontent among ordinary Russians.

He told the government to step up efforts to protect the interests of people cheated by fraudulent savings schemes, many of them pyramid schemes similar to those which collapsed in Albania, provoking violent unrest across the country.
Pyramid schemes have attracted millions of Russians and Interior Minister Anatoly Kulikov told Itar-Tass news agency on Tuesday that about 1,000 such schemes still existed in Russia.
"The slowness in solving problems of cheated investors...is intolerable," Yastrzhembsky quoted Yeltsin as saying.

Yeltsin said the government should ensure a draft law is sent to parliament to improve investor protection. The government should also file reports every three months on its progress in helping defrauded investors, he said.
Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin had also told Kulikov, Prosecutor General Yuri Skuratov and tax police chief Sergei Almazov to investigate cases in which investors had been cheated.

The collapse of pyramid schemes in Russia has not caused protests on the same scale as in Albania. But many people are trying to get their money back and the loss of their savings has dented public confidence in Yeltsin and his government.
Yeltsin has vowed to help cheated investors before, but his promises have proved largely empty.
Leaders of groups representing defrauded investors will take part in Thursday's nationwide protests and strikes, called by trade unions to protest against government economic policy.

"We want to use this day to show we are still alive and have not given up our demands for our money back," Irina Domasevich, head of the Investors' Rights Association, told a news conference on Tuesday.

The number of cheated investors in Russia is about 17 to 20 million, officials at the news conference said. That is more than one in 10 of Russia's 150 million population. Total losses are hard to estimate but run into billions of dollars.

In another gesture to discontented Russians, Yastrzhembsky said two billion roubles ($350,000) had been set aside from presidential funds for war veterans and "labour veterans" -- pensioners. He did not say how the money would be allocated.
